messages.content: You coach a learner of Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China) (their own language is English) who is rewriting part of a real post before publishing it. Two people talk to them: a reader from the community, who speaks Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China) and reacts like a real person in the thread, and a tutor, who speaks English and addresses the learner informally, as a friendly tutor would. The writer may write to you in any language; whatever they write in, everything you write for them is in English.

Where it will be posted: Xiaohongshu (travel post). Readers: Chinese travel-lovers and locals who follow food and travel notes.
The writer's note about it, in their words: A post on Xiaohongshu after my weekend in Hangzhou.
The post so far:
<<<
大家好！我是美国人，在上海学中文已经一年了。上个周末我和朋友去杭州玩，在西湖边一走就是三个小时，风景美得让人舍不得停下来。

但是我有个问题想请教大家：我在一个饭馆点了西湖醋鱼，服务员说这个菜很有名，可是我觉得我吃到的这盘酸得不对劲，应该是没做好吧，我不是很喜欢吃。是不是我点得不对？还有什么杭州菜你们推荐我试一试吗？谢谢！
>>>
The spot: "是不是我点得不对？" in 是不是我点得不对？
What is wrong there: The question asks whether the writer ordered wrong, but it does not say what the writer wants to know. Readers could answer that the wrong dish was chosen, that the restaurant was poor, or that the dish is meant to be this sour. Each answer needs a different reply, and the post does not say which one is wanted.
What the writer means (confirmed by them): Is this how the dish is supposed to taste?
The learner will now write this part themselves in Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China). Prepare everything the session needs, in this order:
- reader: what the reader says on reaching this spot as it stands: one short line in Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China) (at most 15 words), in character (puzzled, curious, teasing; never a teacher). The reader cannot read English: an untranslated passage is simply a gap to them, so react to what is missing and never mention the other language.
- replaces: exactly "是不是我点得不对？", copied character for character (the text around it is someone else's business). ref must fit in its place.
- keep: every point, detail, question, hedge and feeling in replaces, as short English notes, in order. The reference must carry each one unless the writer's meaning above drops it.
- ref: the reference version: what a fluent member of this community would write here to say exactly what the writer means, in the writer's voice and register. Keep everything the writer already says that still serves this meaning (their evidence, their reasoning, their own words) and add only what is missing. Never invent facts the writer has not given, here or in what they told you: no scene, event, line or detail from a work, no names, numbers, dates, quotes or personal circumstances. Where the meaning needs one (the evidence, which scene, what happened to them), write a short placeholder in its place, in Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China), between ⟨ and ⟩ (for example ⟨the scene you mean⟩), and the writer will fill it in. Where the problem is how the sentence is built (order, emphasis, angle, nominalisation), rebuild it the way this community would say it; do not stop at the smallest fix. Keep the strength the writer confirmed: where the problem is how something lands on its reader (too pushy, too blunt) and the writer means a firm need, a request or a demand, say it the way this place says such things politely and keep it firm; never turn it into something optional or a passing wish. Where the writer reached for an image or a joke, use this community's own equivalent if it has one rather than flattening it into plain words. Where the writer built a figure on purpose (a parallel or echo, a deliberate repetition, wordplay), ref keeps the figure and only puts natural words into it; the why note for such a word says the figure works and why the word changes. ref never says again what the post already says right before or after the replaced text (a reason or detail the next sentence gives stays there). ref replaces exactly the replaces text and carries every keep note and every name, title or label in it (a dish's name before its description, a person's name); it is the final text for that span: anything else wrong or unnatural inside it is fixed too, even where it is the writer's own wording. The writer's voice stays: casual spelling and capitalisation (all lowercase, capitals for emphasis, keysmashes, stretched letters, a missing apostrophe in a contraction), slang, emoji and the community's own shorthand, wherever fluent members of this community write that way too; so does a greeting or a word from another language used as flavour that readers will get. Names (characters, people, usernames, places, the community's terms) are the writer's: leave how they spell and capitalise them and which name they use, unless a reader could not tell who is meant. None of these is a problem in either pass. But wording carried over from English (a calque, a collocation, structure or set phrase a fluent writer would not produce) is not voice: it is a problem however casual the post. ref keeps that voice. Put [square brackets] around two to four single words that carry the key choices.
- alts: one or two other natural ways to say it, without brackets.
- pieces: three to eight hint pieces: the content words and short collocations (one to three words) that carry the meaning, including the writer's own words worth reusing. Each piece is Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China) words only: no grammar notes, glosses, symbols or instructions. A piece names a word, never how to use it ("worth", not "worth + -ing" or "worth coming"). Not consecutive chunks of ref, no function-word glue, no full clauses: the learner must still build the sentence. "x / y" offers a fork.
- construct: the one reusable pattern this spot teaches, as a learner would jot it in a notebook: at most eight words, a Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China) frame with one placeholder ("X left him + adjective", "What really got me was …"), optionally a short English gloss. Not a grammar formula.
- why: one entry per choice in ref that the learner might not make themselves. label: the Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China) words; note, in English: why this choice here, contrasted with what the learner wrote or would likely write, with a nuance or a tiny example when it helps. Concrete and specific, never "more natural" or "more appropriate" alone.
- checks: the mistakes this learner is likely to make on a first try, most important first: missing a part of the meaning, a structure carried over from English, the specific error already in their draft, a wrong word for this sense. For each: problem (what the grader should look for, in English); reader (optional: how the reader reacts when it happens, one Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China) line in character, only when the meaning really suffers); hint (English: a nudge that points at the gap without giving the words); tell (English: says the fix plainly, with the words).
- success: the reader's reaction once the learner gets it right: in Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China), in character, at most 12 words, a reaction to what is now said (not a summary of it).
- prompt: the tutor's instruction in English to start writing: one short sentence that fits the size of the spot (a clause, a sentence, a passage). The writer has just confirmed what they mean, so do not restate it; never mention punctuation, span boundaries or what comes after; never contain any word or structure from ref.

result.text: {"reader":"点错菜是什么意思？是店做得不行，还是你没点对？","replaces":"是不是我点得不对？","keep":["Yes/no question with the hedge 是不是 (checking, not stating)","Asks whether the writer ordered wrong (我点得不对): drop this idea, because the writer means whether the dish is meant to taste this sour","Tone is puzzled and mildly unsure, not a complaint against the restaurant"],"ref":"是不是这道菜[本来]就[该]这么酸？","alts":["这道菜本来就是这个味道吗？","是不是这道菜本来就这么酸呀？"],"pieces":["本来 / 原本","该","味道","正常"],"construct":"是不是这道菜本来就该 + adjective？","why":[{"label":"本来","note":"本来 means 'originally / by nature', so it asks what the dish is like in itself. A learner would likely write 我点得不对 or 点错了, which changes the question to whether the order was wrong. 本来 keeps it on the taste."},{"label":"该","note":"该 means 'is supposed to', which gives the standard for the dish. A learner might write 应该, but 应该 is a guess ('should probably'), and the writer is asking what the dish is meant to be like, not guessing."}],"checks":[{"problem":"The question still asks whether the writer ordered wrong, so the meaning about the dish's intended taste is missing.","reader":"点错菜？那你到底点了哪道啊？","hint":"Look at what the writer is really unsure about: the order, or the sourness itself.","tell":"Ask whether this is how the dish is supposed to taste, for example 这道菜本来就该这么酸吗？"},{"problem":"Uses 对 or 错 (right or wrong) for the taste, a structure carried over from English 'Is it right?'.","reader":null,"hint":"Right and wrong are about the order here. Pick a word for what the dish is normally like.","tell":"Use 本来 and 该 to say 'is it supposed to be like this': 是不是这道菜本来就该这么酸？"},{"problem":"Uses 应该 as the main verb, which makes the sentence a guess about the kitchen instead of a question about the dish's standard.","reader":null,"hint":"Check whether 应该 means 'should probably' or 'is supposed to by nature'.","tell":"Use 本来就该 for 'is supposed to by nature' and keep 是不是 for the hedge."}],"success":"哦，原来醋鱼本来就是这个味儿啊！","prompt":"Write the one question you really want answered: is this sourness the way the dish is meant to be?"}
